The Lion and the Wolf
One winter evening, a wolf was searching for food. He met a lion carrying a large deer. The wolf said, "If we work together, we can share the food and always stay safe." The lion agreed. For many days, they hunted and ate well. But the lion noticed that the wolf always took the biggest portion and rarely helped. One day, the lion said, "Partnership means giving as well as taking. You have taken too much — I will hunt alone from now on." The wolf soon went hungry, while the lion continued living well by himself.
What is the deeper message the writer wants to convey through this story?
choices: Strong animals should not help weaker ones
True partnership requires fairness and equal contribution
You should always work alone to save time
Wolves are cleverer than lions when hunting
Friends should always share everything equally regardless of effort

soal.title:
The Old Clock
In a quiet village, there lived a girl named Elara and her grandfather. High on the wall hung an old wooden clock that had belonged to her great-grandfather. It no longer told the correct time, and the villagers often said, "Why keep something that doesn't work?" But Grandfather would smile and say, "It doesn't need to tell time to tell a story."
One stormy night, Grandfather fell ill. The doctor arrived late because the roads were flooded. Elara sat beside her grandfather, feeling helpless. Then she noticed something — inside the old clock, there was a small hidden compartment. Inside lay a map and a letter written by her great-grandfather. The letter explained a shorter, safer path through the hills that few people knew. Elara followed the map and guided the doctor back in time. Because of that old "useless" clock, her grandfather recovered.
Read each statement carefully. Write T if the statement is TRUE and F if it is FALSE according to the story and its intrinsic elements.

rows.label: The setting of the story — a quiet village on a stormy night — is important because it creates the situation that leads to the main problem.
The main conflict is between the villagers and Elara's grandfather because they disagree about the clock's value.
The clock serves as a symbol — it represents family history, hidden wisdom, and things that are valuable beyond what we can see.
The characterization shows that the grandfather kept the clock simply because he was too lazy to throw it away.
The ending supports the theme that something that seems useless may actually hold the greatest value when we look deeper.

soal.title:
The Enchanting Labuan Bajo
Labuan Bajo is a stunning coastal town situated at the western tip of Flores Island, in East Nusa Tenggara, Indonesia. Over the last few decades, it has transformed from a humble fishing settlement into a vibrant tourism hub and the main gateway to Komodo National Park — a UNESCO World Heritage Site established in 1991.
Blessed with breathtaking natural beauty, the town rests along a peaceful bay surrounded by rolling green hills and sparkling turquoise waters. From Puncak Amelia, visitors are rewarded with a magnificent panoramic vista of the harbour, traditional boats, and scattered islands stretching toward the horizon. One of its most celebrated natural wonders is Tangsi Beach, widely known as Pink Beach. Its distinctive blush hue comes from microscopic red coral fragments that wash ashore and blend naturally with the fine white sand.
Labuan Bajo holds a truly unique treasure — the Komodo dragon, the world’s largest living reptile, found nowhere else on Earth. Beyond its wildlife, the destination enchants visitors with dramatic sunsets, rich Manggarai traditions, and an emerging culinary scene featuring freshly caught seafood. While tourism brings economic prosperity, local communities and authorities strive to preserve the area’s pristine environment and cultural heritage. Labuan Bajo thus represents a delicate balance — one where human progress and nature’s wonders can thrive side by side.
Based on the text, which of the following statements are TRUE about Labuan Bajo?

rows.label: It lies on the western end of Flores Island
Komodo National Park became a UNESCO site in 2001
It was originally a simple fishing village
It is located in West Nusa Tenggara

soal.title:
The Garden of Wishes
The sun smiled gently over Lila’s small garden. Flowers danced in the soft morning breeze. The roses were red as fire, and the jasmine spread like sweet perfume across the yard. But the old oak tree in the corner was a giant guarding the place. Its roots were thick ropes holding the earth together. One day, a heavy storm arrived. The wind was a roaring beast that shook the whole house. Yet the old oak stood strong, whispering courage to the frightened flowers. When morning came, the garden was safe, and the tree stood like a quiet hero.
Read each statement. Write T if TRUE and F if FALSE based on the text.

rows.label: "The sun smiled gently" is an example of personification because it gives a human action to something that is not human.
"Flowers danced in the soft morning breeze" uses a metaphor to compare flowers to dancers.
"The roses were red as fire" is a simile because it uses the word "as" to make a comparison.
"The wind was a roaring beast" is an example of a simile because it compares two things without using "like" or "as".
*"The old oak stood like a quiet hero" uses a metaphor because it says the tree actually is a hero.

soal.title:
Proportion of Fast Food in Daily Calorie Intake in Children and Teenagers
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, over a third of children and teens eat fast food nowadays. Previous studies have shown how fast food can increase the risk of weight gain due to the increased calorie intake, but provide overall poorer quality in individual diet.
Teenagers gained weight due to increased fast food intake, according to a previous survey included in a Centers for Disease Control and Prevention report. According to the survey, teens with excess body fat were at increased risk of many common cancers, including post-menopausal breast, colorectal, and liver cancer.
The report also found that 34 percent of 2- to 19-year-olds eat fast food daily, and about one in ten children gets a quarter to 40 percent of their calories from fast food.
These results show us that children and teenagers who consume a lot of fast food will risk developing chronic disease later in life. Melissa Halas-Liang, a registered dietitian, advised, "Parents don't need to feel overwhelmed. They can take simple steps to choose healthier fast food items if they are too busy and make healthier choices that are fast and easy at home." Here are three things parents can do to provide healthy food for their children.
Prepare a healthy pre-cooked meal in the freezer for a quick last-minute home-cooked meal. Soups, chili, and even stir-fried dishes can be stored in the freezer. A healthy dinner is just a microwave away.
Canned foods can create a quick meal with minimal clean-up. Add frozen vegetables to a canned soup or try canned salmon or tuna with hummus and mayo served with whole grain crackers and baby carrots. Try and opt for canned foods with less sodium if possible.
If you stop by a fast food court, look for healthier options. Choose baked or grilled over fried or crispy. Add healthier sides like baked potatoes, salad, or warm soup over fries.
In conclusion, fast food consumption may mean an increased risk of chronic disease later in life. Parents can take simple steps to make sure their children eat healthily. Various countermeasures can be taken to promote convenient, but still healthy eating.
Classify each item into the correct category based on the two texts above.

A quick and healthy meal using canned salmon or tuna

Meals that are ready to heat and eat quickly

rows.label: Prepare pre-cooked meals and store them in the freezer

Over one-third of children and teens eat fast food nowadays

soal.title:
Happy and Sympathetic Expressions in Conversation
People use different kinds of expressions to show how they feel and how they respond to others. Expressions of happiness are used when something good happens or when we want to celebrate with someone. Examples include: "I’m so happy for you!", "Congratulations!", "I’m really pleased to hear that!", "How wonderful!", and "Great job!" Using these expressions makes others feel valued and supported.
On the other hand, expressions of sympathy are used when someone experiences something unpleasant, sad, or difficult. These expressions show that we care and understand their feelings. Common expressions include: "I’m so sorry to hear that.", "Please accept my deepest sympathy.", "How terrible.", "I hope things get better soon.", and "I’m here if you need anything." Using kind words during difficult times can comfort others and strengthen relationships.
It is important to know the difference between these two types of expressions and when to use them appropriately. We congratulate people on their success, and we offer comfort when someone faces misfortune. Using the right expression at the right time shows good manners and empathy toward others.
Which of the following expressions show happiness or congratulations?
choices: I’m so sorry to hear that.
Congratulations on your success!
How terrible!
I’m really happy for you!
I hope you feel better soon.

Every day, in kitchens and dining areas across every household around the world, we use a wide variety of items to prepare, serve, and enjoy our meals. Utensils include spoons, forks, spatulas, bowls, and plates — the tools that help us handle food safely and conveniently. While they may seem simple, these objects are made from many different materials, each with its own qualities and environmental impact. Wood, bamboo, ceramic, metal, glass, and plastic all serve us well, but they behave very differently once we are finished using them.
When these items are damaged, worn out, or no longer needed, they turn into waste — but not all waste is created equal. Organic waste such as leftover food, fruit peels, and vegetable scraps naturally decomposes over time, returning valuable nutrients back into the soil. In this way, nature creates a continuous cycle of renewal. However, synthetic materials like plastic and styrofoam do not break down easily. They can persist in the environment for hundreds of years, accumulating in landfills, rivers, and oceans, where they harm wildlife and pollute ecosystems.
Understanding the difference between utensils, materials, and waste is more than just learning definitions — it is about understanding the impact of our daily choices. When we choose reusable utensils instead of single-use ones, we reduce the amount of waste we create. When we sort our waste carefully, we allow valuable materials to be recycled rather than lost forever. A cleaner world begins not with grand changes made by others, but with small, thoughtful decisions made by each of us, every single day.

soal.title:
Plastic Pollution in Indonesia — A Growing Challenge
Indonesia is one of the world’s most beautiful archipelagos, home to thousands of islands and rich coastal ecosystems. Yet it also faces one of the most serious environmental challenges of our time: plastic pollution. Every year, Indonesia produces millions of tons of plastic waste. A large portion of this waste does not reach proper disposal sites — instead, it is left behind in rivers, carried by currents into the ocean, or buried in the ground where it does not easily break down.
Single-use plastics are the biggest part of the problem. They are convenient and cheap, yet they are often used for only a few minutes before being discarded. Because plastic does not decompose naturally like organic waste, it can persist in the environment for hundreds of years. Over time, sunlight and waves break it down into tiny microplastics that enter the water, the soil, and even the food chain. Marine animals such as sea turtles, fish, and seabirds frequently mistake plastic items for food, which can cause injury, illness, or even death.
However, the situation is not hopeless. Across Indonesia, communities, schools, and local governments are taking meaningful action. They are reducing single-use plastics, improving waste collection, and raising public awareness. What makes this issue truly complex is that solving it requires more than just cleaning up — it means changing habits, redesigning products, and thinking about long-term consequences. The choices we make today will determine whether Indonesia’s oceans remain pristine or become overwhelmed by waste in the future.

soal.title:
Waste Sorting in Indonesia — A Cleaner Future
Indonesia is a beautiful country with rich natural landscapes, from lush rainforests to stunning coastlines. However, like many nations around the world, it faces a growing challenge: managing waste properly. To protect our environment, many communities across Indonesia have started using a simple yet effective system — separating waste into three main groups using three coloured dustbins.
The green dustbin is for organic waste. Over time, these materials decompose naturally and turn into compost, which helps grow healthy plants and gardens. They are nature’s own way of recycling.
The yellow dustbin holds items that can be processed and used again — recyclable waste. When these materials are collected separately, they can be turned into new products instead of taking up space in landfills. This saves energy and precious natural resources.
The red dustbin is for non-recyclable waste — items that cannot be reused or recycled easily. Although these items cannot be recycled, keeping them separate helps keep other waste clean and makes the sorting process more hygienic.
By sorting waste correctly, every person in Indonesia can make a real difference. It may seem like a small step, but when millions of people do it together, it creates a cleaner, healthier country for us all.

soal.title:
The Old Mangrove and the Fisherman
High on the coast of Kampung Laut stood an old mangrove tree that had watched over the village for generations. Pak Damar, a fisherman, passed it every day on his way to the sea. Once, the forest stretched far and wide, but over the years, people cleared large areas to build shrimp ponds. The water became murky, storms grew stronger, and the fish began to disappear. Villagers grew worried — the very thing they had gained was slowly taking away what they loved most.
One year, a powerful storm swept across the coast. While other parts of the village suffered damage, the area around the old mangrove remained safe. Pak Damar realized the truth: the trees they had almost forgotten were their strongest protection. He began persuading others to restore the forest. Many doubted it would work, saying it would take too long and earn no money. But Pak Damar did not give up. Year after year, they planted saplings, protected the young trees, and waited.
Twenty-four years later, the mangrove forest had returned. The water cleared, the fish came back, and Kampung Laut became famous across the islands for its mangrove seedlings. Visitors came from far away to learn from them. The old mangrove still stands there — not just as a tree, but as a quiet reminder: what we save today saves us tomorrow.

soal.title:
The Green Transformation of Bantay Village
High in the hills lies Bantay Village, a place surrounded by beautiful forests and clear rivers. For generations, the people here lived in harmony with nature. However, as the years passed, the forests became thinner and the rivers grew dirtier. The air was not as fresh as it once was, and the seasons felt less predictable than before.
The village elders knew they had to act. "A healthy forest is important for our future," said Elder Lito. "It is more important than earning quick money by selling our trees." At first, some families disagreed. They believed cutting down trees for farms would bring greater wealth than keeping the woods standing.
Slowly but surely, the community came together. They planted thousands of young trees and protected the riverbanks. They learned that a living forest is more valuable than timber sold at the market. After many years, the results were clear: the forest grew thicker, the water ran cleaner, and wildlife returned. Today, among all the villages in the region, Bantay has become the most prosperous and the most peaceful place to live. It proves that caring for the environment is the wisest choice we can ever make.

Container Gardening — Growing Green in Small Spaces
Context: The villagers of Bantay are discussing a new way to grow food without clearing more land — container gardening. They share different ideas and opinions about it.
Kania: We don’t have much open space left for big gardens. In my opinion, container gardening is a brilliant solution. We can grow vegetables in pots, old buckets, and wooden boxes right on our porches.
Shabila: I completely agree with you. It means we don’t need to cut down any trees or clear new land. Plus, it’s easier to water and take care of plants that are close to our homes.
Nurul: I see what you mean, but I don’t entirely agree. Containers have limited soil, so plants might not grow as big or produce as much as they would in the ground. I think we should still keep some traditional garden beds too.
Maulana: Personally, I believe container gardening is worth trying first. Even if the harvest is smaller, it’s better than having no fresh vegetables at all.
Soimah: I couldn’t agree more with Kania. It also gives people who live in houses with no yard a chance to grow their own food. That’s wonderful!
Wisnu: I respectfully disagree with the idea that it’s better than traditional farming. It takes a lot of time to water and maintain many small containers. From my point of view, we should focus on one shared community garden instead.
Kania: I get your concern, but I still think both methods can work together — containers for herbs and small vegetables, and a shared garden for larger crops.

soal.title:
The Cleanest Cities in the World

Surabaya — A Proud, Clean City in Indonesia
Surabaya, the provincial capital of East Java, has exemplified a remarkable commitment to environmental sustainability and cleanliness. It is situated on the eastern coast of Java.
The city has comprehensive recycling programs and regular garbage collection which contribute to creating a pristine environment.
Even though the capital of East Java ranks behind Jakarta in terms of population size, it is not a second-class city. Surabaya is an award-winning city. It was voted as the top tourism destination at the 2018 "Yokatta" Wonderful Indonesia Tourism Awards. Surabaya also won a Special Mention at the 2018 Lee Kuan Yew World City Prize in recognition of its urban development strategy. The strategy boosted the economy of the city rapidly with minimal pollution to the environment. Green spaces make up more than one-fifth of the city's area, which has about 100 parks scattered around it.
Moreover, Surabaya's inhabitants actively participate in cleanliness and community clean-up efforts. They also foster environmental awareness and responsibility. The local authorities and the community always try to uphold cleanliness standards. They maintain its streets, parks, and public spaces carefully.
Surabaya is one of the cleanest cities in Indonesia. It is well-known not only for its cleanliness but also for its environmental stewardship. The city has just received an achievement for keeping the city clean and orderly, the Adipura Kencana Trophy. Surabaya has been given the award due to its relentless commitment to maintaining pristine surroundings and sustainable living practices for residents and visitors.
World's Cleanest Cities
Singapore: Known for its strict cleanliness laws and efficient waste management system, Singapore is often considered one of the cleanest cities in the world.
Copenhagen, Denmark: Copenhagen is renowned for its focus on sustainability and environmental initiatives, including extensive cycling infrastructure and green spaces.
Osaka, Japan: Osaka has a strong culture of cleanliness and order, with well-maintained streets and public spaces.

soal.title:
Proportion of Fast Food in Daily Calorie Intake in Children and Teenagers
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, over a third of children and teens eat fast food nowadays. Previous studies have shown how fast food can increase the risk of weight gain due to the increased calorie intake, but provide overall poorer quality in individual diet.
Teenagers gained weight due to increased fast food intake, according to a previous survey included in a Centers for Disease Control and Prevention report. According to the survey, teens with excess body fat were at increased risk of many common cancers, including post-menopausal breast, colorectal, and liver cancer.
The report also found that 34 percent of 2- to 19-year-olds eat fast food daily, and about one in ten children gets a quarter to 40 percent of their calories from fast food.
These results show us that children and teenagers who consume a lot of fast food will risk developing chronic disease later in life. Melissa Halas-Liang, a registered dietitian, advised, "Parents don't need to feel overwhelmed. They can take simple steps to choose healthier fast food items if they are too busy and make healthier choices that are fast and easy at home." Here are three things parents can do to provide healthy food for their children.
Prepare a healthy pre-cooked meal in the freezer for a quick last-minute home-cooked meal. Soups, chili, and even stir-fried dishes can be stored in the freezer. A healthy dinner is just a microwave away.
Canned foods can create a quick meal with minimal clean-up. Add frozen vegetables to a canned soup or try canned salmon or tuna with hummus and mayo served with whole grain crackers and baby carrots. Try and opt for canned foods with less sodium if possible.
If you stop by a fast food court, look for healthier options. Choose baked or grilled over fried or crispy. Add healthier sides like baked potatoes, salad, or warm soup over fries.
In conclusion, fast food consumption may mean an increased risk of chronic disease later in life. Parents can take simple steps to make sure their children eat healthily. Various countermeasures can be taken to promote convenient, but still healthy eating.
